messages.subject: Re: [pdf plots] Ancestral state in black
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- apologies that I totally missed this -- but black I think indicates the null state, which suggests you are running the so-called "DEC*" model which removes the null range from the state space.  An estimate of e=5 suggests this also, since typically e heads to infinity when the null range is excluded (see full discussion in Massana et al on bioRxiv).

Switching to standard DEC with include_null_range=TRUE should fix the general issue, or changing the plot_BioGeoBEARS_results input to have include_null_range=FALSE should fix the plotting issue with DEC*. (from memory)

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Cannot plot figures ...
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- probably you are running the part of the code that opens a PDF for writing, e.g.:

#######################################################
# PDF plots
#######################################################
pdffn = "Psychotria_DEC_vs_DEC+J_M0_unconstrained_v1.pdf"
pdf(pdffn, width=6, height=6)

...but not the part of the code that closes the writing of the PDF, and then opens the PDF for viewing...

dev.off()  # Turn off PDF
cmdstr = paste("open ", pdffn, sep="")
system(cmdstr) # Plot it

Just type dev.off() a couple of times to close any previously-opened PDFs/graphics devices, then either (a) do all of the PDF opening/closing commands, or (b) skip the PDF-related commands to plot to the R graphics window.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- it's this issue:

check_BioGeoBEARS_run() says: STOP ERROR: 1 row(s) of the BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table are set to be 'free', but they have starting values ('init') outside of the specified min/max.

...this can happen e.g. if pieces of the example script are run out of order, or something similar.

Like the message says, type:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table

...then see which "free" parameters have an initial starting value ("init") outside of the allowed "min" or "max".  Then change the init value or the min or max to fix it.

# E.g. to lower the min of "j" to 0.00000000001:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"] = 0.00000000001

Cheers!
Nick

Hi - "works" just means a parameter is usable or not, not whether it is used. Ignore mx01r, it is a vestige of a long-lost idea.

The error you were hitting is that BioGeoBEARS does a check: for every free parameter, is its "init" in-between its "min" and "max".

If you hit that error, you need to change init, min, or max, nothing else.  The "works" column is not relevant.

As with everything, when starting out it is safest to

1. Go back to the example script
2. Switch in your input files
3. Run the script without changing anything, and being careful not to skip lines.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- probably just change it once on the BAYAREALIKE+J model setup, for *only* the parameter that is outside the bounds.

Normally the defaults avoid this min/max issue, and the example script does as well.  What happened is that you deleted or skipped some chunk of the example script, such that when the "min" is raised on j for BAYAREALIKE+J:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"] = 0.00001

I have run it and I see the error now:

d free    5 1e-07   5   5 works anagenesis: rate of 'dispersal' (range expansion)
Error in check_BioGeoBEARS_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object) :
  check_BioGeoBEARS_run() says: STOP ERROR: 1 row(s) of the BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table are set to be 'free', but they have starting values ('init') outside of the specified min/max.

===========

Your BAYAREALIKE analysis estimated "d" at 5.0, which becomes the starting value of "d" for the BAYAREALIKE+J analysis, but the "max" for "d" in BAYAREALIKE+J is set to 4.9999999.  So, as the error message says, the starting value is outside the specified min/max.

Estimating "d" above 5 is pretty rare, that would mean expecting >5 events per millions of years, typically most trees have branch lengths of millions of years and an average less than 1 event per branch.  It may be that some of the super-short branches in your tree cause this.

Anyway, you would never want to report an estimate of 5 anyways, because that isn't the actual maximum likelihood estimate, it's just the upper boundary on your allowed parameter space.

The solution is just to raise the max, I've done this for both models, see attached script -- have to run to class but I bet it will work now. Search "NJM" for my edits.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] pseudo-Bayesian
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- I don't fully get what you are asking, but if you have:

* substanstial uncertainty about the tree topology/dating
* several different manual dispersal multiplier matrices you want to test

...then you could

(a) take e.g. 50 trees, run your model set (say, DEC with 3 different matrices, DEC+J with the same 3 matrices = 6 models, 6 models times 50 trees = 300 runs)

(b) you could sum the lnLs or AICs across the 50 trees for each model, take the average, and see which of the 6 models is best. I don't think there is any exact statistical theory for this, unless you moved all the way to a full Bayesian analysis, but it would give you a decent idea

Another, perhaps preferable analysis, would be to run the whole standard model comparison on each individual tree, and then just say "DEC+J+matrix3 wins for 41/50 trees, DEC+matrix2 wins for 9/50 trees" or whatever.

None of this would tell you "which route fits best" -- even under the best model, there may be a bunch of possible dispersal histories -- use Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping to visualize/describe them -- but they would tell you how much the statistical model comparison varies by tree.

Cheers!
Nick

Em sex., 20 de ago. de 2021 às 00:38, Nick Matzke <nickmat...@gmail.com> escreveu:

> Hi -- I don't fully get what you are asking, but if you have:
>
> * substanstial uncertainty about the tree topology/dating
> * several different manual dispersal multiplier matrices you want to test
>
> ...then you could
>
> (a) take e.g. 50 trees, run your model set (say, DEC with 3 different matrices, DEC+J with the same 3 matrices = 6 models, 6 models times 50 trees = 300 runs)
>
> (b) you could sum the lnLs or AICs across the 50 trees for each model, take the average, and see which of the 6 models is best. I don't think there is any exact statistical theory for this, unless you moved all the way to a full Bayesian analysis, but it would give you a decent idea
>
> Another, perhaps preferable analysis, would be to run the whole standard model comparison on each individual tree, and then just say "DEC+J+matrix3 wins for 41/50 trees, DEC+matrix2 wins for 9/50 trees" or whatever.
>
> None of this would tell you "which route fits best" -- even under the best model, there may be a bunch of possible dispersal histories -- use Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping to visualize/describe them -- but they would tell you how much the statistical model comparison varies by tree.
>
> Cheers!

Hi Nick: Thanks for the assistance ... will try and replicate on my end so as to test the various models. With regards to biogeographic units, here's an FYI ...

We're evaluating mtDNA cyt-b sequences for Snowtrout (a cyprinid fish) endemic to the Tibetan Plateau and (subsequently) SE Asia. The samples thus represent the 7 large rivers (and their tribs) that originate on the Plateau and disperse south and east.

 Our Lab samples fill the void that exists for SNT in the Central Himalaya (i.e., Nepal/ Bhutan), and thus serves to link the Plateau proper/ the trans-Himalaya/ major SE Asian rivers. We have examined our samples using ddRAD but (obviously) must fall back to GenBank data for a comprehensive examination of fish evolution across the Plateau ... /M.
